title: Spring Lecture #31: JPA Cascading, Lazy Loading & N+1 Problem
sources: code/jpaRelationshipDemo (Student, Department, Profile, repositories, StudentService, DepartmentService)

questions.question: If you write a relationship annotation without a `fetch` attribute, which pair of mappings is EAGER by default according to JPA?
options: `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany`
`@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne`
`@OneToMany` and `@OneToOne`
All four relationship annotations are EAGER unless marked LAZY
questions.explanation: JPA defaults to-one associations (`@ManyToOne`, `@OneToOne`) to EAGER and to-many associations (`@OneToMany`, `@ManyToMany`) to LAZY. That is why the lecture code explicitly writes `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)` and `@OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)` on `Student`.

questions.question: You are deciding where to put `CascadeType.REMOVE`. Which relationship is the safest candidate for it?
options: `Student.courses` (`@ManyToMany`), so deleting a student also cleans up the courses
`Student.department` (`@ManyToOne`), so deleting a student removes the department
Every relationship in the project, so no orphan rows are ever left behind
`Order.items` (`@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")`), because an order item has no meaning without its order
questions.explanation: Cascade REMOVE fits when the child belongs exclusively to the parent, like order items. Courses and departments are shared by many students, so cascading a student's deletion to them would wipe out data other students still reference.

questions.question: In the lecture's `Student`, both `department` (`@ManyToOne`) and `profile` (`@OneToOne` with `@JoinColumn(name = "profile_id")`) are `FetchType.LAZY`. Student 1 exists and the persistence context is empty. How many SQL SELECT statements does this method execute?
options: 1 - only the student row is selected; the getters return uninitialized proxies
2 - the student, plus one SELECT for the department when `getDepartment()` is called
3 - one SELECT for the student and one for each getter call
1 - a single SELECT that joins student, department and profile
questions.explanation: With LAZY to-one associations Hibernate selects only the student row (including the `dept_id` and `profile_id` FK values) and puts proxies in the fields. Getting the reference alone does not initialize a proxy; only reading real state such as `getName()` would. There is no join because nothing requested the associations.

questions.question: The database has 100 students spread over exactly 3 departments. `Student.department` is `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)` and no batch fetching is configured. How many SQL queries does this method run?
options: 1, because `findAll()` always joins the to-one associations
101, one for the students and one per student
4, one for the students and one per distinct department
3, one per department, because the student list comes from the cache
questions.explanation: One query loads the students; then each distinct department proxy is initialized once and reused from the persistence context for the other students that reference it, giving 1 + 3. The notes stress that this is still the N+1 pattern: the first-level cache only removes duplicate primary-key lookups, it does not fix the fetch plan.
questions.source: notes p13-15 (N+1, First-level cache and the exact query count)

questions.question: Why do the notes say that switching `Student.department` to `FetchType.EAGER` is NOT a reliable fix for N+1?
options: EAGER is only a hint, so Hibernate usually ignores it and keeps loading lazily
EAGER only guarantees the data is available; Hibernate may still use secondary selects, and the eager load applies to every use case, even ones that don't need it
EAGER disables the first-level cache, so every department is loaded once per student
EAGER works only on `@OneToMany`, so on `@ManyToOne` it has no effect
questions.explanation: In JPA, EAGER is a requirement (LAZY is the hint), but it does not dictate one join query: a list query can still trigger secondary selects per parent. It is also a global mapping choice that loads the association everywhere. The recommended approach is LAZY by default plus a query-level fetch plan.
questions.source: notes p9, p16-17 (Does N+1 mean lazy loading is bad?)

questions.question: Your student-list endpoint only shows id and name, but the student-report endpoint prints every student's department and profile, and SQL logs show repeated SELECTs inside the loop. Following the lecture's principle, what is the best design?
options: Keep `department` and `profile` LAZY in the entity and add a Spring Data repository method annotated `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"department", "profile"})` for the report
Change both associations to `FetchType.EAGER`, since the report always needs them
Add `cascade = CascadeType.ALL` to both associations so they are loaded with the student
Turn off `spring.jpa.show-sql` in production, because logging is what makes the report slow
questions.explanation: The notes recommend keeping relationships lazy by default and fetching the required graph explicitly per use case. An entity graph on the report method adds those associations to that query's fetch plan without bloating the list endpoint. Cascade controls lifecycle operations, not loading, and EAGER would load the associations for the list endpoint too.
questions.source: notes p16, p18-19 (Preventing N+1 with an Entity Graph)

questions.question: In the lecture project, `StudentRepository` is a plain class that uses `EntityManager`. A developer tries to add an entity graph like this. Which statement is correct?
options: It works: `@EntityGraph` is applied to any method of a bean annotated with `@Repository`
It works, but only if the method is also annotated with `@Transactional`
It fails at startup because `@EntityGraph` requires a `@NamedEntityGraph` on `Student`

`@EntityGraph` is processed by Spring Data's repository proxies, so here it is ignored; declare `List<Student> findAll()` with the annotation in an interface that extends `JpaRepository<Student, Long>`
questions.explanation: `org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph` is read by the Spring Data JPA repository infrastructure when it runs query methods of a repository interface. In a hand-written class, the JPQL runs with the mapping's defaults (LAZY), so the N+1 remains. Ad-hoc `attributePaths` graphs do not need a `@NamedEntityGraph`.

questions.question: In the lecture's day-31 project, `Department` no longer has a `students` collection (it is commented out), while `Student` keeps `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(name = "dept_id")`. `DELETE /api/department/5` calls `entityManager.remove(department)` for a department that still has students. What happens?
options: Hibernate first sets `dept_id = NULL` on the students, then deletes the department
Hibernate deletes the students first because `@ManyToOne` cascades REMOVE by default
The DELETE on the department row violates the students' foreign-key constraint, so the flush fails and the transaction rolls back
Nothing happens, because `remove()` is ignored for entities that are referenced by others
questions.explanation: No cascade is enabled by default, and Hibernate does not automatically clear foreign keys that other rows hold. The database rejects deleting a department that `student.dept_id` still references. To delete it, you must first reassign or delete the students (or deliberately cascade REMOVE when children truly belong to the parent).

questions.question: For an admin report, a teammate adds `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"students", "courses", "projects"})` to fetch several large collections in one repository call. Why do the notes warn against this?
options: Entity graphs can only contain one attribute path
Joining several collections multiplies the rows (a Cartesian-like product), producing a huge result with many duplicated parent rows at the SQL level
Collections in an entity graph are always loaded lazily anyway, so the graph has no effect
Fetching collections in a graph turns them into EAGER mappings for the whole application
questions.explanation: Each joined collection multiplies the number of result rows: with 50 students, 10 courses and 5 projects, one parent can come back as 2,500 rows. Entity graphs do accept multiple and nested paths, and they affect only that method's fetch plan, not the global mapping.
questions.source: notes p19-20 (Fetching multiple attributes, nested attribute paths)

questions.question: `Order.items` is `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)` and `OrderItem.order` is `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")` (nullable). `addItem` is the notes' helper (`items.add(item); item.setOrder(this);`). What is stored after commit?
options: One order and two items, both with `order_id` set to the new order's id
One order and only item `b`; item `a` is skipped because it was not added through the helper
One order and two items; `b` has the order's id but `a` has `order_id = NULL`
An exception, because `a` is in the collection but does not reference the order
questions.explanation: Cascade PERSIST follows the `items` collection, so both new items are persisted. But the FK value comes from the owning side `OrderItem.order`, which was only set for `b`. This shows the notes' point: cascade manages lifecycle, while helper methods keep the owning side (and the FK) correct.
questions.source: notes p1-3 (Cascade does not mean relationship ownership)
